title: How A Crisis Can Turn A CEO Into A Leader

entries.quote: As a leader, dealing with a crisis starts with getting clear on what you know and don’t know.
entries.advice: In a crisis, first separate facts from unknowns, and go past your direct reports to the front-line staff who hold the information.

entries.quote: It’s critically important to communicate quickly and clearly during a crisis—with the board, employees, customers and partners.
entries.advice: Tell your board, staff, customers and partners what is happening, fast and plainly; how you communicate either rebuilds trust or destroys it.

entries.quote: But the right thing to do is the exact opposite, which is to communicate early and communicate often.
entries.advice: When you discover bad news like a breach, resist waiting for certainty; share what you know right away and keep updating people.

entries.quote: you need to make decisions so quickly that you literally take them and move forward.
entries.advice: In a crisis, decide almost instantly and keep moving rather than deliberating.

entries.quote: In these situations, you don’t have the luxury of giving other people work. Sometimes you just have to take it on yourself.
entries.advice: When a crisis hits, do the urgent work yourself rather than handing it off.

entries.quote: You just can't waver in those situations. You just have to show confidence, even when you may not have 100% of it yourself.
entries.advice: Project steady confidence to your team during a crisis, even while you privately have doubts.

entries.quote: One of my mentors once told me to never fail to take advantage of a crisis.
entries.advice: Use a crisis to push through big changes, since people accept change far more readily then.

entries.quote: But we did create a crisis playbook to follow just in case it ever happened again.
entries.advice: After an incident, write down a response playbook so you're ready if it ever recurs.

title: How To Be Successful With Distributed Teams

entries.quote: First time founders will especially need advisors and coaches that have been there before
entries.advice: As a first-time founder, line up advisers and coaches who have already built companies to guide you.

entries.quote: The key to avoiding this pitfall is to assume a remote-first culture when considering company processes and norms.
entries.advice: Design every company process and norm as though the whole team works remotely.

entries.quote: The biggest risk to building distributed teams probably isn’t lost productivity today, but rather employees feeling disconnected from their coworkers.
entries.advice: With a distributed team, worry less about output and more about people feeling cut off from colleagues.

title: PagerDuty IPO And The Next Billion Dollar Category: Apps-As-A-Platform

entries.quote: But as it gained traction, PagerDuty recognized an opportunity to move beyond its initial offering to build a platform.
entries.advice: Once your pain-solving product gains traction, look for ways to expand beyond it into a platform.

title: The Secret Behind Slack's Runaway Success

entries.quote: What sets Slack and Zoom apart: both have cracked the code of distribution.
entries.advice: Don't stop at a product that solves real pain; figure out distribution, which is what separates category leaders.

entries.quote: Product-led GTM mirrors the mechanics of consumer goods — the buyer is the end-user and must be able to derive value from the product quickly.
entries.advice: For product-led growth, make sure end users get value fast, can research the product themselves, and pay a low price.

entries.quote: While these companies could let their product do the talking early on, as they continued to scale, a robust sales force became essential.
entries.advice: Even if viral product adoption carries you early, plan to build a strong sales team as you scale.

entries.quote: Your product should be a great source of leads, but it will never be the entire funnel.
entries.advice: Treat product usage as one lead source, not your whole pipeline, and make sure the product gives users value immediately.

title: What Surviving An Arctic Snowstorm Taught Me About Running A High Growth Startup

entries.quote: Instead of being decisive this time around, I maintained a mirage of growth.
entries.advice: When acquisition costs climb and churn rises, act decisively instead of keeping up an illusion of growth.

entries.quote: it dawned on me that instead of acting boldly as CEO, I had been running on fear too often.
entries.advice: Notice when fear of letting down your team or investors is steering your decisions, and choose bold action instead.

entries.quote: Rather than acting invincible, I needed to be vulnerable and open about the company’s situation.
entries.advice: Be candid about where the company really stands instead of projecting invincibility.

entries.quote: I went to my board and provided a clear view on where we stood and what I saw as our path forward.
entries.advice: Bring your board an honest picture of the current situation along with your proposed plan forward.

entries.quote: Instead, they appreciated my candor, clarity, and vision. Again, they urged me to move quickly and boldly.
entries.advice: Level with your board; candor, clarity and vision tend to earn backing for fast, bold action.

entries.quote: But it also takes great partners who can help you in the good times and the bad times.
entries.advice: Choose investors and partners who will help through hard stretches, not only when things go well.

entries.quote: I suspect it’s because the model relies on employees adopting tools that change their workflow and often threaten their own utility.
entries.advice: Expect slow uptake if your AI tool asks employees to change workflows in ways that threaten their own jobs.

entries.quote: Buyer: End user (misaligned) → Management (aligned)
entries.advice: Sell AI that does the work to management, whose incentives line up, rather than asking end users to adopt it.

entries.advice: Charge for your product instead of giving it away to monetize through ads; genuine value will get customers to pay.

entries.advice: Be ready to change product, business model and target segment at once, such as moving to large enterprises signing $100K-plus deals.

entries.advice: Remember small customers can cost as much to sell as large ones; aim where your fit is and hire people who can sell there.

entries.advice: Be willing to move from inside sales to direct selling, supported by account management and professional services.

entries.quote: This is why it’s so important to work on conveying your ideas and expectations with clarity.
entries.advice: Practice communicating ideas and expectations clearly and consistently; without that, even capable people can't be put to good use.

title: Future of AI Investing

entries.quote: From zero to one, the most important signal is how quickly the founding team is learning.
entries.advice: At the earliest stage, show investors how fast your founding team learns; that pace is the signal they weigh most.

title: Future of Enterprise

entries.quote: Now buyers want specific AI teammates and want to buy a complete service, not just the technology.
entries.advice: Sell a complete AI service aimed at a specific job; buyers have moved away from do-it-yourself technology.

entries.quote: The rules are being rewritten, and founders need to adapt their go-to-market playbooks just as fast as their products.
entries.advice: Skip the big SDR team; rework your sales and marketing approach as fast as you rework your product.

title: Scrunch: From AI Agent Experience Platform to Sitecore Acquisition

entries.quote: having a people-first focus and a long-term commitment and looking to surround yourself with sort of great people along the way.
entries.advice: Show investors shared values: you put people first, you are in it for the long haul, and you keep great people around you.

entries.quote: you did everything we would ever want as an investor, which is you put your heart and soul into the company
entries.advice: Commit fully to your company even when the path is winding and unclear; that total commitment is what investors want.

title: What Claude Code Can (and Can’t) Replace

entries.quote: Autonomous agents create a new security boundary. You need sandboxing, scoped credentials, and audit trails to survive enterprise scrutiny.
entries.advice: Give your agents sandboxes, narrowly scoped credentials and audit logs so they pass enterprise security reviews.

entries.quote: Sell outcomes, not software. Offer throughput guarantees, accuracy SLAs, and reduced operational risk.
entries.advice: Package your product as guaranteed results, with commitments on throughput, accuracy and lower risk, instead of as a tool.

entries.quote: Pursue a regulatory moat. Agents can’t get licensed, certified, or audited.
entries.advice: Look for regulated work where licensing, certification and audits demand accountable humans that agents can't supply.

title: A Founder’s Leadership Reading Guide

entries.quote: Show up early. Every time. Respecting time is the first step in respecting your team.
entries.advice: Arrive early to everything; respecting people's time is where respect for your team begins.

entries.quote: Don’t make excuses. Own the miss.
entries.advice: When you fall short, take responsibility without explaining it away.

entries.quote: Set clear goals and objectives. Ambiguity is the enemy of execution.
entries.advice: Give your team unambiguous goals, because vagueness undermines getting things done.

title: Annual Planning Playbook for Startup CEOs

entries.quote: Annual planning begins with revisiting the mission, objective, and strategy. This is the CEO’s job.
entries.advice: As CEO, open annual planning yourself by re-examining why you exist, what you aim to achieve, and how you will win.

entries.quote: You want a model that reflects reality (pipeline, conversion, churn, margins) and constraints (cash, runway), supports your strategy, and is aspirational.
entries.advice: Build a financial model grounded in real pipeline, conversion, churn, margin, cash and runway figures that still stretches the team.

entries.quote: Founders should use the planning process to define the 3–5 key priorities for the business next year, along with the key initiatives that support them.
entries.advice: Set three to five company priorities with supporting initiatives as a team exercise; people push harder on plans they shaped.

entries.quote: Ideally should begin with a verb and finish in the form of from X to Y by Z
entries.advice: Write each objective ambitious yet specific: lead with an action verb and state a baseline, a target, and a deadline.

entries.quote: Predictive (moves before the lagging result) Influenceable (the team can directly impact it) Ongoing (tracked weekly or monthly)
entries.advice: Pick metrics that move ahead of results, that the team can directly affect, and that you track every week or month.

entries.quote: Have a single executive owner (one throat to choke / one leader to unblock)
entries.advice: Give every priority exactly one accountable executive who can also clear its blockers.

entries.quote: A plan without a cadence is just a document.
entries.advice: Pair your plan with a regular review rhythm, or it will just sit on a shelf.

title: Beyond the Financial Operating Plan: Establishing Your “Theme for the Year”

entries.quote: While you need a financial plan for the board, you need a Theme for the Year for the company.
entries.advice: Alongside the board's financial plan, give the company an inspiring annual theme that drives people to their best work.

entries.quote: We wanted to convince Gartner & Forrester to create a Magic Quadrant and Wave, establishing us as the clear leader.
entries.advice: To lead an emerging category, push the major analyst firms to formally define it with you as the leader.

entries.quote: We demonstrate vision, get to the decision makers, and reshape the prospect’s thinking to win.
entries.advice: Refuse to be one row in a vendor comparison; reach the real decision makers and reframe how the prospect thinks.

entries.quote: Find that theme, define it clearly, and repeat it until it becomes the operating system of your company.
entries.advice: Name the human story behind your numbers, spell it out, and keep repeating it until it runs the company.

title: Finding Product-Go-to-Market Fit (PGMF)

entries.quote: When launching a B2B enterprise software startup, it’s just as crucial to find product-go-to-market fit (PGMF) as it is to achieve product-market fit (PMF).
entries.advice: Beyond proving the market wants your product, prove you can sell and grow it efficiently over the long term.

entries.quote: Be prepared for 6–12+ month sales cycles and field reps earning $250K–$350K on-target earnings (OTE), with quotas in the $1.2M–$1.5M range.
entries.advice: Field-sales motions mean long sales cycles and costly reps, so you need six-figure contract values to pay for them.

entries.quote: You can often succeed with inside sales reps who earn $150K–$250K OTE and carry quotas in the $600K–$1M range.
entries.advice: Consider inside reps with three to five years' experience working from a hub office; they needn't bring a big rolodex.

entries.quote: The mid market segment is probably the best choice for most startups
entries.advice: Lean toward mid-market customers as your target segment, but watch for its pitfalls.

entries.quote: founder led sales is the most common, followed by inside sales reps earning $100K–$200K OTE with quotas in the $400K–$600K range
entries.advice: Sell yourself first; when you add reps, inside sellers at roughly $100K to $200K target pay with $400K to $600K quotas are typical.

entries.quote: As you grow and inevitably move upmarket, you may have to reestablish product-market fit for larger customers.
entries.advice: If you sell to startups, expect their spending to track the funding climate, and plan to re-prove fit when you move upmarket.

entries.quote: Aim for as much self-service as possible—maybe just one or two calls, and a deal cycle of a few weeks at most.
entries.advice: When the user is also a buyer with a credit card, keep selling to a call or two and deals to weeks, with frictionless onboarding.

title: Is Your Startup Built to IPO? Understanding TAM, ACVs, and GTM

entries.quote: For any founder evaluating a new startup idea, determining whether a market is "big enough" is crucial.
entries.advice: During customer discovery, also test whether the market is large enough; founders often skip this, yet it heavily shapes long-term success.

entries.quote: I find those reports to be misleading especially for startups which are often creating new markets.
entries.advice: Don't trust top-down analyst reports to size a market you're creating; reason it out with a simpler model of your own.

entries.quote: Today, to go public you need $200M+ in revenue. Further, market leading companies often only get to 10-15% market share.
entries.advice: Work the math: with about 2,000 target companies and a 10% share, reaching IPO-scale revenue takes deals of $1M or more.

entries.quote: Rabbits: TAM: 1,000,000s ACV: $1K+ GTM: Self Serve w/ Inside AEs w/ $100K OTE and $300K quotas
entries.advice: Match your sales model to deal size: with millions of prospects paying around $1K, run self-serve plus inside reps on modest quotas.

title: Pricing & Packaging Pillars For (AI) Startups: Five Models to Consider

entries.quote: The gains we achieved were largely due to improving the way we priced and packaged the product.
entries.advice: Grow contract values by reworking how you price and package, even without major changes to the core product.

entries.quote: If your AI agent has real variable costs, consider capping usage or layering in fair-use language.
entries.advice: If each use of your agent costs you real money, cap usage or add fair-use terms to the contract.

entries.quote: If your AI replaces people, or if it’s more of an agent than a user tool, you might consider charging per “AI agent” seat.
entries.advice: If your product replaces human workers, price per agent rather than per human user so automation doesn't erode your revenue.

entries.quote: If you go outcome-based, consider a hybrid: a small base fee plus a success fee.
entries.advice: For outcome-based pricing, charge a modest base fee and a separate success fee so slow results don't leave you carrying costs indefinitely.

entries.quote: your best bet is to pick the model that is relatively easy for your target customer to grasp and for you to manage.
entries.advice: Early on, choose a pricing model customers grasp instantly and you can run easily, to keep deals moving; refine it later.

entries.quote: you want to see each customer have a chance to grow 25-50% per year in upsells.
entries.advice: As you scale, test pricing that lifts contract value and net retention, giving each account room to expand 25–50% a year.

entries.quote: Speak the Language of ROI: Whether it’s seat-based or outcome-based, always connect the dots for your buyer: “Here’s how we save/make you money.”
entries.advice: Whatever your pricing model, show buyers exactly how you save or earn them money; that makes higher prices easier to accept.

title: Sales Methodology Simplified: Ditch the Questions, Teach and Share Insights

entries.quote: While this "solution selling" approach might work in some cases (e.g., mature industries with mature products), it's not ideal for startups.
entries.advice: Skip interrogation-style solution selling with prospects; it suits mature markets and products, not a startup.

entries.quote: When you approach a prospect, come armed with perspective, and show them why they're a good fit for your technology.
entries.advice: Draw on your customer interviews and research to teach prospects something new and show why your technology suits them.

entries.quote: The main goal is to get prospects to agree with your insights, recognize their needs, and believe that your technology category can address those needs.
entries.advice: Open sales conversations with insights rather than questions or product demos; first get agreement on the need and your category.

title: Sales Playbook: What is it and How to Establish it

entries.quote: modern sales playbooks aim to teach buyers to see the world in a new way and create demand where it might not have existed.
entries.advice: Build a playbook that creates demand by changing how buyers see their situation, not one built to disqualify prospects.

entries.quote: The sales playbook can be divided into three steps: 1) Confirm Need; 2) Why New Product; 3) Why Company’s Product.
entries.advice: Run sales in order: confirm the buyer's need, then why a new kind of product, and only then why yours.

entries.quote: During the sales cycle, a seller should have a point of view based on research that the prospect likely shares.
entries.advice: Walk into each sales conversation with a researched view and guide the buyer to recognize and agree on their need.

entries.quote: Once the buyer agrees they have a need, the goal is to convince them that your category of product
entries.advice: After the buyer accepts the need, sell your product category before your company, or you'll get lost among alternatives.

entries.quote: To achieve this alignment, provide valuable analysis the customer can use, like scorecards and benchmarks.
entries.advice: Win agreement on the category by giving prospects useful analysis such as scorecards and benchmarks.

entries.quote: Typically, this part of the playbook includes a "review plan" with a 1) Functional Review; 2) Technical Review; 3) Implementation review.
entries.advice: Pitch your own product only after need and category are agreed, then run functional, technical and implementation reviews.

entries.quote: The final stages of the sales playbook are procurement and signature, which, as a side note, often take longer than expected when selling to enterprises.
entries.advice: Leave extra time for enterprise procurement and signing; those final steps usually run long.

entries.quote: The key takeaway is that it's crucial for founders to be involved in establishing a sales playbook.
entries.advice: Stay personally involved in building the sales playbook so it stays rooted in teaching buyers and sharing insight.

title: Startup Defensibility Report Card in the Age of Anthropic & OpenAI

entries.quote: Would the product still matter if you removed the LLM? If nothing meaningful remains, it is probably a prompt, wrapper, or Skill.
entries.advice: Imagine your product with the model removed; if nothing valuable remains, you've built a thin wrapper rather than a product.

entries.quote: Does the product coordinate multiple people? Single-player workflows are easy for better models to absorb.
entries.advice: Build for teams, with roles, handoffs, approvals and shared state; solo workflows are easy prey for stronger models.

entries.quote: The more state the product owns, the harder it is to collapse into a generic agent.
entries.advice: Have your product track decisions, exceptions, approvals and outcomes over time so a generic agent can't replace it.

entries.quote: Static data gets commoditized. Live data from repeated workflows, resolutions, edge cases, outcomes, and performance benchmarks can compound.
entries.advice: Build your data advantage from the live work flowing through your system, not from static data that others can match.

entries.quote: Self-serve tools for everyone are fragile. A considered purchase in a specific vertical, sold with expertise, trust, and clear outcomes, is harder to displace.
entries.advice: Choose a specific vertical and sell an expert-led, considered purchase with clear outcomes rather than a horizontal self-serve tool.

title: The 3 Phases of Enterprise Software Sales Maturity: A Founder's Guide

entries.quote: You'll know you're on the right track when you have a handful of referenceable customers
entries.advice: Treat five to ten reference customers plus a must-have product as your early sign of fit, typically below $1M ARR.

entries.quote: Success here looks like a standardized sales playbook and reps bringing in 3x their On-Target Earnings (OTE) in new annual bookings.
entries.advice: Between $1M and $10M ARR, aim for a standard playbook and reps who each book three times their target pay in new business a year.

entries.quote: To succeed, aim for a repeatable sales model with reps consistently hitting around 80% of their quotas and 2-3x new ACV growth.
entries.advice: When scaling, target a model where reps reliably reach about 80% of quota while new ACV grows two to three times.

title: The AI-Enabled Services Opportunity

entries.quote: Selling AI agents directly into an organization often requires multi-stakeholder buy-in, change management, and anxiety around job displacement.
entries.advice: Expect selling agents straight into a company to stall on aligning many stakeholders, managing change, and fears about jobs.

entries.quote: The enterprise has already decided it doesn’t want to do this work in-house. It already buys the outcome, not the tool.
entries.advice: Target work that companies already outsource; they buy results, so sales cycles are shorter and change management lighter.

entries.quote: the best way to sell agents into the enterprise may be to not sell agents at all.
entries.advice: Consider selling the finished service your agents deliver instead of the agents themselves.

entries.quote: Margin improvement is what AI does out of the box.
entries.advice: Don't rely on AI cost savings as your edge; rivals and incumbents can use identical models on identical work.

entries.quote: Better gross margins are the starting point. Compounding advantages are the company.
entries.advice: Convert how you deliver the service into product, data, deep workflows and customer stickiness; improved margins are just the beginning.

title: The CEO Job Changes After Product-Market Fit

entries.quote: What made you fast early can make the company slow later—because everything routes through you.
entries.advice: Watch for your hands-on habits turning you into a bottleneck as the company scales.

entries.quote: Instead of constantly asking, “What can I do myself?” your job becomes, “Who—or what AI agent—can do this reliably without me?”
entries.advice: Stop asking what you can do yourself; ask which person or AI agent can reliably handle it without you.

entries.quote: Hire great people to do the jobs you used to do.
entries.advice: Hand your old jobs to strong hires, accepting you no longer need to be the best at everything.

entries.quote: When you’re small, effort is the constraint. When you’re scaling, focus is the constraint.
entries.advice: As you scale, guard your focus; it replaces effort as the thing holding the company back.

entries.quote: Repeat the vision and priorities until you’re blue in the face.
entries.advice: Keep restating vision and priorities even when it feels repetitive; one announcement never creates alignment.

entries.quote: Own 1–3 critical initiatives per quarter. Delegate the rest.
entries.advice: Each quarter, personally lead the one to three initiatives that unlock the next growth phase and hand off everything else.

entries.quote: Make a list of everything that currently depends on you. Pick one and redesign it so it no longer does.
entries.advice: List what relies on you, redesign one item at a time, and for weekly tasks decide to hire, delegate or automate.

title: The new Series A is the old Series B.

entries.quote: Today’s A: $3-5M to be competitive, roughly the old B bar.
entries.advice: Plan to reach about $3–5M in ARR before a competitive Series A, the level a Series B once required.

entries.quote: Perhaps the biggest mistake is raising too little at too high of a valuation, usually in the seed round
entries.advice: At seed, don't raise a small amount at a rich valuation; missing the next milestones then makes the following round nearly impossible.

entries.quote: Raise the right amount of money, at a stage appropriate valuation, to hit the milestones that unlock the next stage.
entries.advice: Ignore round labels; size your raise and valuation to fund the specific milestones your next round will demand.

title: Professional Services: The Secret to Scaling Enterprise (AI Agent) Startups

entries.quote: It turns out the final 10% of AI agent implementation is challenging.
entries.advice: Pair your AI agent product with hands-on implementation services, because the last stretch of deployment is the hard part.

entries.quote: Setting this expectation upfront didn't deter customers; it built credibility and demonstrated our understanding of the implementation challenges.
entries.advice: Promise a realistic go-live timeline, such as 90 days, from the start; honest expectations build credibility with buyers.

entries.quote: Enterprises typically expect to spend anywhere from 50-200% of their first-year subscription license cost on professional services
entries.advice: Price implementation knowing enterprises often budget half to twice their first-year license fee for services.

entries.quote: In the early days, PS doesn't need to be a profit center.
entries.advice: Early on, run services at cost or even at a loss if that cuts churn and makes the product stickier.

entries.quote: Longer-term, successful software companies often aim for a gross margin of 15-30% on services
entries.advice: Over time, target 15–30% gross margin on services, supported by roughly 75% utilization and disciplined pricing.

entries.quote: as long as services revenue remains roughly 25-30% of total revenue or less, it won't significantly drag down your multiple.
entries.advice: Keep services at or below about a quarter to 30% of revenue so they don't weigh on your valuation multiple.

title: The SaaSpocalypse CEO Survival Guide: Six Months Later

entries.quote: Path 1: Re-found around an AI-native outcome.
entries.advice: If growth stalls, consider re-founding the company on an AI-native result, even moving to consumption pricing.

entries.quote: 3) Build an AI native development team, as a rule of thumb it’s probably 30% of your current team size
entries.advice: Stand up an AI-native engineering group of roughly 30% of today's headcount, rebuild sales for AI, or else sell the company.

entries.quote: Only option that really doesn’t work? It’s the status quo.
entries.advice: Whatever path you pick, don't stand still; leaving things as they are is the one choice that fails.

title: The SaaSpocalypse CEO Survival Guide

entries.quote: Start planning around 2–3x revenue. That number changes every decision downstream—fundraising, M&A, burn, etc.
entries.advice: Plan on a valuation of two to three times revenue, and let that reset shape fundraising, M&A and burn decisions.

entries.quote: You have distribution—getting contracts into enterprises is hard, and you already have them.
entries.advice: As an incumbent, build your agentic product on the distribution, customer data and trust you already hold.

entries.quote: Stop building new features for the legacy SaaS platform.
entries.advice: Freeze legacy feature work, change how you build for a tenfold output jump, and hire AI-native talent if needed.

entries.quote: You need to solve for agentic orchestration, accuracy and consistency, personality, memory and context, human-in-the-loop control, tool integrations, multi-agent collaboration, and usage or outcome-based billing.
entries.advice: Treat agent building as new work: plan for orchestration, reliability, memory, human oversight, integrations and new billing.

entries.quote: All of this is still being figured out in real time—every new model release reshuffles the deck. This is not a part-time job.
entries.advice: Give your agentic transition full-time attention, since each model release changes the ground under you.

entries.quote: Be willing to give the agentic product away to existing customers.
entries.advice: Hand existing customers the agentic product free if it speeds their switch; a new AI customer is worth far more than a renewal.

entries.quote: No one is going to hand you credit for what you built before. You’re essentially re-founding the company. Suck it up, and go.
entries.advice: Treat an AI pivot as re-founding the company and expect no credit for past wins.

title: How to pitch me: 5 investors discuss what they’re looking for in April 2023

entries.quote: We are actively looking to lead new enterprise software investments, at both inception and Series A stages.
entries.advice: Target investors whose focus fits you, such as funds leading enterprise software rounds at inception or Series A in AI, data or security.

entries.quote: Before pitching investors, founders should talk to customers — not just a handful but tens or hundreds of customers.
entries.advice: Talk with dozens or hundreds of customers before you pitch, so you arrive with context, clarity and conviction.

entries.quote: in Sales 101, what converts even higher than cold outreach is a warm intro, so that always is a better route (but not required)!
entries.advice: Seek a warm introduction to investors when you can; a well-crafted cold email is welcome but converts less.

entries.quote: Startup CEOs should have a sufficient “living salary” to take care of basic needs.
entries.advice: Pay yourself enough to cover basic living costs so money worries don't pull you off the company.

entries.quote: There is no way a founder can be successful and have a second job.
entries.advice: Drop any second job and focus fully on building product and landing customers.

entries.quote: These include setting arbitrary deadlines in an effort to create FOMO.
entries.advice: Don't impose artificial deadlines on investors to manufacture urgency; that bull-market tactic no longer fits.

entries.quote: Another one is setting a specific raise amount and/or dilution targets without context for what investors are looking for.
entries.advice: Don't fix your raise size or dilution without knowing what investors expect; it signals poor awareness of the market.

entries.quote: I have a strong preference for reviewing a pitch deck and have found it greatly increases the likelihood of a second meeting with a founder.
entries.advice: Bring a deck to investor meetings; it explains complex ideas to non-experts and improves your odds of a second meeting.

entries.quote: seeing a founder present a pitch deck allows VCs to evaluate skills that enterprise software entrepreneurs will need for a long time: storytelling and selling.
entries.advice: Present your deck live; investors use it to judge your storytelling and selling, skills you will need for years.

entries.quote: Finally, a pitch deck serves as a useful leave-behind to reference, which increases the likelihood of a next step.
entries.advice: Leave your deck behind after an investor meeting so they can refer back to it and move toward a next step.

entries.quote: Surround yourself with great advisers and early team members, especially those who are experts in areas where you might have less experience.
entries.advice: Recruit advisers and early hires who are strong exactly where you are inexperienced.

title: Mayfield gets a new partner as it celebrates 50 years in the business

entries.quote: Along my journey, I realized how lonely the founder-CEO role can be.
entries.advice: Counter the loneliness of the CEO job by surrounding yourself with supportive people, including investors you trust.

entries.quote: I am hoping to encourage CEOs to take the long view.
entries.advice: Take the long view through good stretches and bad, and don't assume every downturn is your fault.

entries.quote: I also learned so much from being part of a CEO coaching group — both through guidance from the leader and from my peers
entries.advice: Join a CEO coaching group to learn from both its leader and your fellow CEOs.
